evidence.quote: Strip away the biosecurity and cyber-safety PR, and OpenAI’s new “Combatting adversarial distillation” paper is an accidental confession about why closed-API labs are terrified.

Here is the actual technical reality they buried inside their own post. When a student model only sees a teacher’s final answer or a sanitized “reasoning summary,” it learns what token sequence looks plausible. When a student model gets the teacher’s raw, unedited chain-of-thought trace, it gets dense, step-by-step search trajectories: how the teacher
decomposed a hard problem, hit a dead end, backtracked, verified an intermediate hypothesis, and self-corrected before emitting a single final token.

In modern reinforcement learning (GRPO and process-reward pipelines), raw reasoning traces are pure gold because they bypass the most expensive part of frontier post-training: running millions of failed rollouts to discover good search heuristics. Instead of burning $100 million on RL compute exploration, a competitor with a clean dataset of raw CoT

trajectories can run supervised fine-tuning on those exact search paths and immediately warm-start RL at a fraction of the compute budget. OpenAI’s own cyber distillation chart admits this flat out: at higher inference budgets, the student trained on exact reasoning traces beats the summary-trained student even after reinforcement learning.

@boblabs_eu ran Qwen3.8-27B BF16 on an H100 PCIe. The model has about 3.4× as many parameters. Estimated GPU time for an 85-request coding session increased by 0.2%, and measured output throughput fell by 0.5% with four concurrent requests.

@Kairos_Res, would you be up for running the same benchmark on tensorcash:native? Matching the GPU, input and output lengths, concurrency, and model where both stacks support it would make for a useful comparison. I’d love to see throughput and latency with mining on and off.

evidence.quote: One of the best critiques of the RFQ model comes from @chameleon_jeff
RFQ is supposed to let makers quote hard to quote books for retail mainly. But on-chain, nobody can prove they're retail.

So his team asked makers for quotes that stayed valid for 60 to 90 seconds, waited to see where the price went, and only executed the ones that had moved in their favour. Obv, makers cut them off and they had to rotate wallets.
The fix is to give makers last look. But then retail loses the reason to use RFQ in the first place.
